extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and educated readers interested in aesthetics and art theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for what counts as art and good art (definitions of beauty, moral/social function, realism vs theatricality, allowable methods, sensory scope). Useful for artists, critics, and students of æsthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / Realism versus Theatrical Artificiality
rubrics_metrics.description: People do not converse in such a way as recitative, and do not place themselves at fixed distances, in a quartet, waving their arms to express their emotions; nowhere, except in theatres, do people walk about in such a manner, in pairs, with tinfoil halberds and in slippers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the artistic presentation represents believable human behaviour or relies on contrived theatrical conventions. Anti-patterns: fixed, repetitive gesticulation, meaningless processions and artificial staging (e.g. repeated ‘Home I bring the bri-i-ide’ with the same mechanical actions). If the representation is so unlike life that it can't move or be understood, ask 'For whom is this being done?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of Social Cost / No Harmful Sacrifice for Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Art, for the sake of which the labour of millions, the lives of men, and above all, love between man and man, are being sacrificed,—this very art is becoming something more and more vague and uncertain to human perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the social and economic costs of producing an artwork (taxes, subsidies, coerced or degrading labour) are justified by the work’s value. Work that requires or habitually depends on unjust or harmful sacrifices (people selling their only cow to pay for art taxes; unwilling labour) fails this criterion unless its importance clearly redeems the cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and Legitimate Audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinctively the question presents itself—For whom is this being done?... The man of culture is heartily sick of them, while to a real working man they are utterly incomprehensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider for whom the work is intended and whether it actually reaches or communicates to that audience. Art that only serves a narrow elite or is incomprehensible to the broader public should be questioned; clarity of address and communicative efficacy are positive qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Decency (avoidance of lewdness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballet, in which half-naked women make voluptuous movements, twisting themselves into various sensual wreathings, is simply a lewd performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether sexualized or overtly sensual content undermines the work’s moral or æsthetic value. Tolstoy identifies gratuitous sensual display (as in certain ballets) as diminishing art rather than enhancing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality and Humane Methods of Production
rubrics_metrics.description: The director...raps with his stick...I heard the words, 'asses,' 'fools,' 'idiots,' 'swine,' addressed to the musicians and singers... The conductor knows that these people are so demoralised... He therefore gives free vent to his churlishness... because this is the way the best conductors behave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the ethics of rehearsal and production practices. Harsh, humiliating treatment of performers and workers is not justified by tradition or by the supposed greatness of the art; methods should respect collaborators' dignity and be proportionate to the work’s true worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent Critical Standards (avoidance of sectarian contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism, in which the lovers of art used to find support for their opinions, has latterly become so self-contradictory, that, if we exclude from the domain of art all that to which the critics of various schools themselves deny the title, there is scarcely any art left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating works, be wary of relying on sectarian or mutually exclusive critical doctrines. A healthy æsthetics requires coherent, non-contradictory standards; widespread mutual exclusion among critics indicates conceptual confusion rather than a measure of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as Manifestation of Beauty (traditional popular criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is such activity as produces beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many people use 'beauty' as the defining purpose of art. Apply this criterion by asking whether the work manifests beauty, but be cautious: the term 'beauty' is variously defined and often ambiguous; further specification is required (see alternative definitions below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as Sensuous Order / Imitation of Nature (Baumgarten)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is the Perfect (the Absolute), recognised through the senses... Beauty is defined by Baumgarten as a correspondence, i.e. an order of the parts in their mutual relations to each other and in their relation to the whole... the highest aim of art is to copy nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this standard, evaluate formal order, harmony, and faithful imitation of nature. A work that displays well-ordered relations among parts and convincingly reflects natural forms counts highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as Moral Good / Art's Moral Aim (Sulzer, Mendelssohn)
rubrics_metrics.description: They...recognise as the aim of art, not beauty, but goodness. Sulzer says that only that can be considered beautiful which contains goodness... According to Mendelssohn, the aim of art is moral perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess artworks by their capacity to evoke, educate, or advance moral feeling and social welfare. Under this rubric, æsthetic value is tied to ethical content and educative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as External Form and Expression (Winckelmann and followers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law and aim of all art is beauty only... There are three kinds of beauty:—(1) beauty of form, (2) beauty of idea, expressing itself in the position of the figure (in plastic art), (3) beauty of expression, attainable only when the two first conditions are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize formal beauty, idealized form, and expressive unity. This standard favors works that achieve beauty of form and expression (classical ideals, imitation of antique art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterested Aesthetic Pleasure (Kant / Schiller)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty, according to Kant, in its subjective meaning is that which, in general and necessarily, without reasonings and without practical advantage, pleases... In its objective meaning it is the form of a suitable object in so far as that object is perceived without any conception of its utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work produces pleasure that is disinterested (not tied to moral or practical advantage). Artistic value here is the capacity to produce pure æsthetic judgment and pleasure independent of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste / Internal Sense and the Balance of Richness and Restraint (Hutcheson, Home, Hemsterhuis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of beauty consists in evoking in us the perception of uniformity amid variety... Beauty is that which gives most pleasure, and that gives most pleasure which gives us the greatest number of ideas in the shortest time... The standard of true taste is that the maximum of richness, fulness, strength, and variety of impression should be contained in the narrowest limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the work by an internal sense or taste for the harmonious balance of variety and unity. Positive features: richness and intensity of impression combined with restraint and economy of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of the Five Senses / Broad Conception of Art (Kralik, Guyau)
rubrics_metrics.description: He speaks of the æsthetic treatment of the five senses... Die Kunst des Geschmacksinns (The art of the sense of taste)... the art of touch, of hearing, of sight... Guyau: 'If the sense of touch lacks colour, it gives us, on the other hand, a notion which the eye alone cannot afford... In the idea we form of the beauty of a woman, the velouté of her skin enters as an essential element.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize artistic value across sensory domains (taste, smell, touch, hearing, sight). Practices often dismissed (cookery, costume, scent) can be legitimate arts; include sensory impact beyond sight and hearing in evaluation.
